title: Silence and Inventory
premise: Orsen Eastwick, a translator who has spent thirty years erasing the dialect of their childhood from their own tongue, learns that the crumbling house in Marrow Fen where they grew up is being auctioned by a distant cousin. Returning to catalog its contents for the sale, Orsen finds their late mother's notebooks—half in a dying language, half in confession—and must finally confront what happened the winter their brother Denny disappeared and Orsen alone came home. As the auction date closes in and buyers circle the land, Orsen translates the notebooks at last, discovering that silence was never protection but a debt passed down. In the end, Orsen withdraws the house from sale, speaks Denny's name aloud at the fen's edge in the old language, and begins translating the notebooks into a book that gives the vanished words—and the vanished boy—a permanent place in the world.
about_author: Rafael Blackwood is the pen name of a former lexicographer who spent a decade documenting endangered dialects along England's eastern fens before turning to fiction. They write quietly devastating novels about language, inheritance, and the things families bury.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Orsen, working late on a commercial translation in London, reaches for a childhood word for 'dusk' and finds it gone—the third loss that month. POV: Orsen. The beat is quiet dread: memory as a leaking vessel, and the first hint that losing the language means losing something else too.

chapters.title: Letter with a Return Address
chapters.summary: A solicitor's letter arrives: the Eastwick house in Marrow Fen goes to auction in six weeks; as next of kin, Orsen may catalog the contents or forfeit all claim. POV: Orsen. Emotional beat: panic disguised as indifference, and the realization that invisibility has an expiration date.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: On the train north, Orsen reviews the mental ledger they've kept since leaving home—every sentence swallowed, every name unspoken. POV: Orsen. The beat establishes the novel's central metaphor: Orsen has survived by accounting for silence rather than breaking it.

chapters.title: Marrow Fen
chapters.summary: Orsen arrives to find the village half-emptied by flood risk and buyouts, the house sagging but stubbornly standing. A neighbor, Mrs. Calloway, recognizes them instantly: 'You're the one who came back.' POV: Orsen. Beat: shame surfacing in a place where everyone remembers what Orsen won't say.

chapters.title: Room by Room
chapters.summary: Orsen begins the formal inventory—furniture, tools, dust—cataloging objects with clinical precision while avoiding the locked attic stair. POV: Orsen. Emotional beat: control through listing, but each object drags a memory loose against Orsen's will.

chapters.title: Denny's Boots
chapters.summary: In the scullery, Orsen finds their brother's boots, still mud-crusted from the fen, exactly where they were the morning after Denny vanished. POV: Orsen, slipping into flashback. Beat: the past stops being abstract; grief arrives with physical force.

chapters.title: What the Village Remembers
chapters.summary: At the fading pub, locals trade versions of the old story—that the mother drove Denny out, that Orsen saw something, that the fen took him. POV: Orsen. Beat: Orsen realizes the town's memory is a rival narrator, and their silence has let others write the ending.

chapters.title: The Locked Stair
chapters.summary: Orsen forces the attic door and finds boxes of their mother's belongings, including notebooks written half in the fen dialect, half in shaky English. POV: Orsen. Beat: temptation and terror—the confession exists, but reading it means surrendering the silence that kept Orsen whole.

chapters.title: First Page, First Refusal
chapters.summary: Orsen translates a single line—'I know which one of you it was'—and stops, burning nothing only because there's no fire lit. POV: Orsen. Beat: self-preservation versus truth; the reader now knows the notebooks accuse someone, and Orsen fears it names them.

chapters.title: Mrs. Calloway's Version
chapters.summary: The elderly neighbor, sensing Orsen's unraveling, tells her own account of that winter: the mother's rages, Denny's wildness, and how Orsen returned alone, soaked to the waist, saying nothing for three days. POV: alternating Orsen and Calloway. Beat: Orsen's curated memory cracks against witness testimony.

chapters.title: A Buyer Comes
chapters.summary: A property developer surveys the land, offering cash for a quick sale and promising the house will be demolished regardless. POV: Orsen. Beat: external pressure mounts—a deadline now has a face, and letting the house go would mean letting the notebooks burn unread.

chapters.title: The Word for 'Brother'
chapters.summary: Translating further, Orsen discovers the dialect word for sibling carries meanings English lacks—one who shares your drowning. POV: Orsen, with flashbacks of teaching Denny the word. Beat: tenderness resurfaces under guilt; Orsen begins wanting the truth, not just fearing it.

chapters.title: Midpoint: The Winter Recalled
chapters.summary: A full flashback chapter: twelve-year-old Orsen and Denny on the frozen fen the night he went through the ice—or was pushed, or wandered—and Orsen running home without looking back. POV: Orsen. Beat: the central mystery sharpens; even Orsen no longer trusts their own version.

chapters.title: Mother's Handwriting Changes
chapters.summary: Orsen notices the notebooks shift over years—from justification to doubt to something like prayer, the final entries asking forgiveness of 'the one who stayed.' POV: Orsen. Beat: dawning comprehension that the mother's silence toward Orsen was itself a wound, not a verdict.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Orsen drafts the official inventory for the sale and realizes they are doing to the house exactly what they did to themselves: pricing everything, explaining nothing. POV: Orsen. Beat: crisis of identity—the translator who has spent a life converting meaning into safe, sellable blanks.

chapters.title: Rising Tension: The Developer's Deadline
chapters.summary: The buyer moves up his offer date; the solicitor warns that contesting the sale requires proof of the estate's true contents—including anything unpublished. POV: Orsen. Beat: legal machinery forces the question: are the notebooks inventory, evidence, or inheritance?

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Orsen translates the notebook's final page: the mother confesses she followed Denny to the fen that night, that he slipped from her reaching hand, and that she let Orsen carry the blame by never correcting the village. POV: Orsen. Beat: devastation and release—the silence was her sin, not Orsen's.

chapters.title: Climax: Speaking at the Fen
chapters.summary: On the eve of auction, Orsen walks onto the frozen marsh at dusk, finds the thin place in the ice, and speaks Denny's name aloud in the dying language for the first time in thirty years. POV: Orsen. Beat: catharsis—the words come back the moment they're needed, as if the language was waiting to be used honestly.

chapters.title: Withdrawal
chapters.summary: Orsen formally withdraws the house from auction, forfeiting the money, and registers the notebooks as a literary estate rather than chattels. POV: Orsen. Beat: defiance—the price of survival paid back in full, choosing memory over liquidity.

chapters.title: Telling the Village
chapters.summary: Orsen reads the mother's confession aloud in the pub, ending the town's forty-year rumor mill, then visits Mrs. Calloway, who weeps and forgives them both. POV: Orsen. Beat: belonging reclaimed—not by forgetting, but by finally being legible to the people who watched.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Months later in London, Orsen finishes rendering the notebooks into English, keeping the dialect words untranslated where English fails, and titles the manuscript 'Silence and Inventory.' POV: Orsen. Beat: transformation—Orsen becomes not a translator of commerce but a translator of the dead.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Orsen returns one last time to keep the house, now theirs, and reads the finished translation aloud in the empty kitchen to a room holding two brothers' boots and a mother's chair. POV: Orsen. Final beat: resolution—the inventory complete, nothing left unsaid, the language alive because someone finally chose to speak it.
